# Draft:King of Them All: The Story of King Records

----
King of Them All: The Story of King Records is a 2025 American documentary film directed and produced by Yemi Oyediran. The film chronicles the history and cultural impact of King Records, an independent record label founded in Cincinnati, Ohio, in 1943 by Syd Nathan. The documentary examines how the label helped shape rhythm and blues, country, soul, funk, and early rock and roll, establishing itself as one of the most influential independent labels in American music history.
The film premiered nationally on PBS in October 2025 and is distributed through public television platforms, including PBS Passport and YouTube.
Synopsis
The documentary follows King Records from its origins as a modest Cincinnati storefront operation to its emergence as a powerhouse of postwar American music. Founder Syd Nathan pioneered an integrated "all under one roof" approach that allowed the label to record, press, and distribute music with unprecedented speed—a vertically integrated model that gave King Records a competitive edge over larger, more bureaucratic competitors.
Through archival footage, rare photographs, and interviews with musicians, historians, and industry veterans, the film brings to life the careers of artists who defined their genres: James Brown's revolutionary funk, Little Willie John's pioneering soul vocals, Hank Ballard's boundary-pushing rhythm and blues, and the Stanley Brothers' influential bluegrass recordings. The documentary also spotlights producer and songwriter Henry Glover, whose behind-the-scenes contributions were crucial to the label's distinctive sound.
The film makes a compelling case for Cincinnati's unique role in American music history. Positioned between North and South, the city became a meeting point for Black and white migration streams and the musical traditions they carried. This geographic and demographic crossroads enabled King Records to build a roster that crossed racial and genre boundaries at a time when segregation dominated American life.
Production
Yemi Oyediran directed and produced the documentary through Afrochine, a Cincinnati-based production company he co-founded with JP Leong. The project required years of development, involving painstaking archival research, complex music rights negotiations, and extensive interviews with artists, scholars, and music industry professionals who could speak to King Records' legacy.
Oyediran not only served as the film's director but also as principal producer and researcher, leading the historical documentation and restoration process. The film was edited by Ed Carson, with art direction by Michelle D'Cruz and cinematography by JP Leong. As part of post-production, the production team restored and enhanced archival photographs and footage, including the application of historically informed colorization using machine-learning techniques developed specifically for the project. These colorizations were then enhanced by Yohance Brown.
The production team drew from an impressive range of sources, including private collections, institutional archives, and vintage broadcast materials. Interview subjects include country music star Vince Gill, acclaimed jazz bassist Christian McBride, legendary music executive Seymour Stein, James Brown's longtime manager Alan Leeds, musicologist Tammy L. Kernodle, and King Records historian Jon Hartley Fox, each offering distinct perspectives on the label's influence.
Much of the post-production effort focused on restoring and contextualizing rare visual and audio materials spanning the 1940s through the 1970s. These archival elements—including performance footage and studio recordings—provide an intimate window into the label's creative process and cultural moment.
Themes
The documentary wrestles with the complex racial dynamics of mid-century American music. King Records created remarkable opportunities for integration during the segregation era, bringing Black and white musicians together in the studio and marketing to both Black and white audiences when such crossover appeal was commercially risky. The film explores how music could transcend social barriers even when society itself remained divided.
Syd Nathan's story illuminates the challenges and possibilities of independent entrepreneurship in an industry dominated by major labels. His vertically integrated business model allowed for creative risks and rapid responses to musical trends that larger corporations couldn't match. The documentary shows how this independence translated into artistic freedom for musicians who might otherwise have been constrained by commercial formulas.
The film also examines how King Records became a crucible for American musical evolution. Country, blues, gospel, and folk traditions—carried to Cincinnati by migrants from Appalachia and the Deep South—converged and cross-pollinated at the label. This cultural exchange produced new hybrid forms that would reshape popular music for generations.
Throughout, the documentary works to recover forgotten histories, highlighting contributions from lesser-known artists, session musicians, and industry figures whose work has been overshadowed by more famous names. It argues for Cincinnati's place as a vital but underappreciated site in the geography of American music, a city whose local scene had national and international reverberations.
Release
King of Them All: The Story of King Records premiered on PBS in October 2025 as part of the network's documentary programming. The film received a national broadcast and was made available through PBS Passport, the network's streaming service for members.
Following its initial broadcast, the documentary was released on YouTube and promoted through public media outlets and press coverage.
Reception
The film has received widespread critical acclaim, with reviewers positioning it among the finest music documentaries ever produced. Critics and music historians have highlighted the documentary's exceptional depth of research, narrative clarity, and its ability to balance comprehensive historical detail with engaging storytelling, making the King Records story accessible to both music scholars and general audiences.
Influential music industry critic Bob Lefsetz praised the documentary enthusiastically, writing that he "could watch this sh*t all day long" and describing it as a "must-watch." He noted that despite initially having no intention of watching the entire film, he "couldn't turn it off," describing it as "a window into the way it once was" that brings the 1950s alive. Lefsetz particularly appreciated the documentary's educational value and its approach to history, noting it avoids the typical hagiography of modern music documentaries since Nathan is deceased and had no hand in the production.
Adam Buckman of *MediaPost* described the film as one of the best documentaries on any subject he has watched, praising it as "hugely entertaining, fascinating and surprisingly moving." He commended the documentary's persuasive thesis about King Records' impact on music evolution in the 1950s and 1960s, noting that it successfully demonstrates the label had as much influence as better-known labels such as Chess, Sun, and Stax. Buckman highlighted the film's jaw-dropping archival materials and praised Oyediran's directorial debut as "very impressive," stating that "a great deal of work was put into this one-hour documentary, and every minute shows it."
John Anderson of The Wall Street Journal offered similarly enthusiastic praise, describing how the documentary places King Records within the broader history of American popular music and highlighted its treatment of Cincinnati as a central element of the story, noting how the film elevates both the label and the city to their rightful place in music history. Billboard published a feature examining the documentary's account of King Records' influence on early rock and roll and popular music.
The documentary's treatment of Syd Nathan has been commended for its nuanced approach. Rather than presenting a simple hagiography, the film acknowledges Nathan's difficult personality and demanding management style while recognizing his genuine commitment to the music and the artists he recorded. Buckman noted the documentary's portrayal of Nathan as "brash, ambitious and opportunistic" but emphasized his colorblind approach to talent and business. Reviewers have also praised the attention given to figures who typically receive little recognition in music histories, revealing the collaborative nature of the label's achievements and recovering voices that had been lost to time.
Accolades
In January 2026, Oyediran received a nomination for the NAACP Image Award in the Outstanding Directing in a Documentary (Television or Film) category for his work on the film. The nomination placed him in a competitive field that included Questlove. The 57th NAACP Image Awards ceremony was scheduled for February 28, 2026, with a live broadcast on BET and CBS.
The project was selected as one of 10 films from 500 submissions to [https://www.pbs.org/about/producing-pbs/open-call/ PBS's Open Call for Emerging Filmmakers] initiative, which supports early- and mid-career filmmakers from underrepresented communities.
